examDifficulty.heading: Is the MuleSoft Integration Foundations Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: This is the gentlest MuleSoft exam. It tests whether you understand the ideas and the vocabulary, not whether you can build. If you have done the Trailhead material and can explain what each part of Anypoint Platform is for, you are most of the way there.
bullets: 40 multiple-choice questions in 70 minutes, which is a comfortable pace.
70% to pass, which is 28 correct answers.
Concepts, not code. You need to recognise what things do, not write DataWeave from scratch.
No experience required. General IT background plus the Trailhead trail is enough for most people.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Work through the MuleSoft Integration Foundations trail on Trailhead and make sure you can explain API-led connectivity in your own words. Aim for 80% or more on practice tests, since the questions are short and the pass mark is 70%.

examFormat.heading: MuleSoft Integration Foundations Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test centre. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: About a third of the questions are short scenarios. The most common one describes an integration need and asks which API-led layer it belongs to, or which Anypoint Platform tool you would use.
bestWayToPass: Learn the three layers: System APIs talk to back-end systems, Process APIs combine data and apply rules, Experience APIs shape data for one app or channel.
Know what each tool is for: Anypoint Studio to build, Exchange to share and discover, API Manager to secure and control, Runtime Manager to deploy and monitor.
Understand the integration styles: Point-to-point, hub and spoke, ESB, and API-led, and why point-to-point gets messy as systems are added.
Recognise the basics of a Mule app: A flow starts with a source, then processors act on the message as it passes through.

certificationCard.description: This entry-level exam covers the basics of API-led connectivity, what each part of Anypoint Platform does, and the integration vocabulary you need to work on a MuleSoft project.

keyConcepts.h2: MuleSoft Integration Foundations: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: API-Led Connectivity and Anypoint Platform
blocks.body: **API-led connectivity** is MuleSoft's way of organising integrations so they can be reused. **System APIs** sit in front of one back-end system, such as SAP or a database, and hide its details. **Process APIs** combine data from several System APIs and apply business rules, for example building a full customer view. **Experience APIs** shape that data for one consumer, such as a mobile app or a partner portal. The point is reuse: the next project calls the existing API instead of building a new connection. On Anypoint Platform, **Anypoint Studio** is where developers build, **Exchange** is the catalogue where APIs and connectors are published and found, **API Manager** applies security and traffic rules, and **Runtime Manager** deploys and monitors the running apps.

blocks.heading: Mule Applications: Flows and Messages
blocks.body: A Mule application is made of **flows**. Each flow begins with a **source**, which is the thing that starts it, such as an HTTP listener receiving a request or a scheduler firing on a timer. After the source come **processors**, which act on the message in order: transform it, route it, call another system, or log something. The data travelling through is the **Mule event**, which carries the **payload** (the content), **attributes** (information about it, like HTTP headers) and **variables** you set along the way. You do not need to write this from memory for the exam, but you should recognise the parts when you see them.

blocks.heading: DataWeave Basics
blocks.body: **DataWeave** is the language used to transform data in Mule, for example turning JSON into XML or renaming fields. A script starts with a header that sets the output type, then a body that builds the result. You should recognise that DataWeave is for mapping and transformation rather than for business logic, and be able to spot a simple transformation when it is shown to you. The exam does not expect you to write complex scripts.

blocks.heading: Connectors and Integration Patterns
blocks.body: **Connectors** are prebuilt components for talking to a particular system, such as HTTP, Database, Salesforce, SAP or Workday. They are published in **Exchange**, where teams also publish their own reusable assets. Know the common integration styles and their trade-offs. **Point-to-point** connects two systems directly, which is quick at first but becomes unmanageable as systems multiply. **Hub and spoke** and **ESB** route through a central component. **API-led** uses layered, reusable APIs, which is the approach MuleSoft recommends.

blocks.heading: Deployment and API Management
blocks.body: A Mule application has to run somewhere. **CloudHub** is MuleSoft's managed cloud, where Salesforce runs the infrastructure for you. **Runtime Fabric** runs applications on your own infrastructure while still being managed centrally. A **customer-hosted** runtime means you install and manage everything. Once an API is running, **API Manager** sits in front of it and applies **policies** such as requiring a client ID, enforcing OAuth, or limiting how many calls a consumer may make. Those limits can be grouped into **SLA tiers** so different consumers get different allowances.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the MuleSoft Integration Foundations Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions ask what something is for. If you can say which layer an integration belongs to and which tool does which job, most answers follow.

blocks.heading: Integration Styles
blocks.body: Point-to-point, hub and spoke, ESB and API-led. Know why point-to-point stops scaling once several systems share data.

blocks.heading: Anypoint Platform Tools
blocks.body: Studio builds, Exchange shares, API Manager secures and limits, Runtime Manager deploys and monitors.

blocks.heading: API Basics
blocks.body: Know what an API is, how REST and SOAP differ, and that a specification describes an API before it is built.

blocks.heading: DataWeave
blocks.body: Recognise simple transformations and remember that DataWeave maps and reshapes data.

blocks.heading: Connectors and Exchange
blocks.body: Connectors talk to specific systems and live in Exchange alongside reusable assets other teams can use.

nextCertsAfter.intro: Good next steps after MuleSoft Integration Foundations:

sampleQuestions.question: A company needs one API that reads customer data straight out of its SAP system and hides SAP's complexity from everyone else. Which API-led layer does this belong to?
sampleQuestions.explanation: System APIs sit in front of a single back-end system and present its data in a simpler, reusable form.
whyWrong: Process APIs combine data from several systems and apply business rules.
The point of the layer is to provide a reusable API over SAP.
Experience APIs shape data for one app or channel.

sampleQuestions.question: A mobile app needs customer data formatted specifically for small screens, drawing on data that existing APIs already provide. Which layer fits?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Experience APIs shape existing data for one particular consumer, such as a mobile app.
whyWrong: System APIs front a single back-end system.
A new database would duplicate data that already exists.
Process APIs combine and apply rules, rather than tailoring output per channel.

sampleQuestions.question: Where do teams publish and discover reusable APIs and connectors?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Exchange is the catalogue where APIs, connectors, templates and examples are published so others can find and reuse them.
whyWrong: Studio is the development environment where applications are built.
API Manager applies security and traffic policies.
Runtime Manager deploys and monitors running applications.

sampleQuestions.question: Which tool would you use to require a client ID and limit how many calls a consumer can make to an API?
sampleQuestions.explanation: API Manager applies policies such as client ID enforcement, OAuth checks and rate limiting.
whyWrong: Studio is for building applications, not applying runtime policies.
Exchange shares assets, it does not enforce traffic rules.
DataWeave transforms data.

sampleQuestions.question: Six systems each connect directly to every other system, and every change breaks something. What is this pattern called, and what does MuleSoft recommend instead?
options: Hub and spoke, replaced by direct calls
sampleQuestions.explanation: Direct links between every pair of systems is point-to-point. It grows unmanageable, which is the problem API-led connectivity addresses with reusable layered APIs.
whyWrong: That reverses the two: API-led is the recommended approach, not the problem.
An ESB is a central routing approach, and file transfers are not the recommended replacement.
Hub and spoke routes through a central point, and direct calls would make things worse.

sampleQuestions.question: What starts a Mule flow?
options: A policy applied in API Manager
A source such as an HTTP listener
sampleQuestions.explanation: Every flow begins with a source: the component that receives a request or fires on a schedule.
whyWrong: DataWeave transforms data inside the flow.
Policies control access to a running API.
Connectors talk to systems, but the flow is started by its source.

sampleQuestions.question: What is DataWeave used for?
options: Transforming data from one shape to another
Deploying the applications out to CloudHub
sampleQuestions.explanation: DataWeave is MuleSoft's transformation language, used to map and reshape data such as JSON to XML.
whyWrong: Monitoring is Runtime Manager's job.
Publishing to Exchange is a separate step.
Deployment is handled by Runtime Manager or the deployment tooling.

sampleQuestions.question: A company wants MuleSoft to run its applications in a managed cloud without maintaining servers. Which deployment option fits?
sampleQuestions.explanation: CloudHub is the managed cloud runtime, where the infrastructure is run for you.
whyWrong: Studio is a development tool, not a runtime.
Exchange is a catalogue of assets.
A customer-hosted runtime means the company installs and manages it themselves.

sampleQuestions.question: Which part of a Mule event carries information about the message, such as HTTP headers?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Attributes hold metadata about the message, such as headers and query parameters, while the payload holds the content.
whyWrong: The payload is the content itself.
Variables hold values you set during the flow.
The flow name identifies the flow, not the message.

sampleQuestions.question: A bank must run Mule applications inside its own data centre but still manage them centrally through Anypoint Platform. Which option fits?
options: Anypoint Studio running on a local machine
sampleQuestions.explanation: Runtime Fabric runs applications on the customer's own infrastructure while keeping central management.
whyWrong: Studio is for building, not running production applications.
Exchange stores and shares assets.
CloudHub runs in MuleSoft's cloud, not the bank's data centre.

sampleQuestions.question: Why does API-led connectivity encourage reuse?
options: It stops teams from building APIs
New projects call existing APIs instead
It replaces every system with MuleSoft
It stores all data in one database
sampleQuestions.explanation: Because APIs are layered and published, the next project consumes what exists rather than integrating from scratch.
whyWrong: It encourages building reusable APIs, not fewer of them.
MuleSoft connects systems rather than replacing them.
API-led does not consolidate data into a single database.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the difference between REST and SOAP APIs, at the level this exam expects?
options: REST is only for databases; SOAP is only for files
REST uses JSON; SOAP uses XML and a WSDL
sampleQuestions.explanation: REST is the lighter, JSON-based style used by most modern APIs. SOAP uses XML with a WSDL contract and is common in older enterprise systems.
whyWrong: They are different styles with different formats and contracts.
SOAP is the older of the two.
Neither is limited to databases or files.

sampleQuestions.question: A scheduled job must pull new orders from a database every 15 minutes. What starts that flow?
sampleQuestions.explanation: A scheduler fires on a timer, which is how flows run on a schedule rather than on request.
whyWrong: An HTTP listener waits for an incoming request.
Policies protect APIs, they do not start flows.
DataWeave transforms data once the flow is running.

sampleQuestions.question: Which statement about connectors is correct?
options: They replace the need for APIs
They have to be written fresh for every single project
Prebuilt components for specific systems, in Exchange
sampleQuestions.explanation: Connectors handle the details of communicating with a particular system and are distributed through Exchange.
whyWrong: Connectors are how APIs reach systems, not a replacement for them.
There are connectors for many systems, including databases, SAP and Workday.
Prebuilt connectors exist precisely so teams do not start from scratch.

sampleQuestions.question: A company wants different call limits for its free and paying API consumers. What should be used?
sampleQuestions.explanation: SLA tiers let you define different allowances and assign consumers to them, enforced by API Manager.
whyWrong: DataWeave transforms data, it does not limit traffic.
Exchange shares assets rather than enforcing limits.
Duplicating the application per consumer is unnecessary and hard to maintain.
